power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The role of financial resources in subjective well-being is extensively studied, yet with many unresolved debates on the precise association, inflection points, or applications.

Using multidimensional data from 91 countries (N=53,589), we find near-universal support for a positive association, which is strongest in wealthier countries and, globally, highly elastic as household incomes surpass local costs of living.
Uniquely, we observe a "psychological inheritance", where the strongest associations are determined by economic class in childhood, even after significant upward mobility by adulthood.
We also find inelasticity in well-being at the top and bottom of income distributions, which largely indicates satiation and decoupling at wealth extremes.
Across countries, well-being surpasses average at household incomes around 4.5 times the cost of living.

Downward mobility is linked with substantial declines but likewise better outcomes than those of equivalent adult incomes that started lower economically, suggesting a psychological endowment where starting point and relative stability are as vital as growth, though the association is strongest in wealthier countries.

The link between income and well-being is therefore strongly supported while personal financial history and broader economic environment have substantial impacts on how money relates to happiness, and thus, to individual and population well-being.
Enabling, protecting, promoting, and advancing the well-being of individuals and communities is the ultimate priority for national prosperity.
Such outcomes may directly impact economic circumstances for individuals and populations (Occhipinti et al., 2023 (Occhipinti et al., , 2023;; WHO, 2025).

text.text: Thus, a comprehensive alignment of where effects and lack of associations between income and wellbeing exist is of utmost importance.
If specific inflection points exist, precision around those plateaus can be critical to identify policy levers and needs.

However, simply incorporating a broader, contextualized understanding of both constructs will better provide a necessary set of insights to leverage that genuinely, as opposed to vaguely, could impact well-being.
Ideally, that broadness includes diversity in both measurements and in analytical approaches to paint a complete picture rather than rely on or base adamant conclusions on a single finding.
To address those questions, we analyzed data from a global survey on mental, financial, and social well-being (research questions are articulated in full in Supplement 2.0.0 and 3.0.0).

Our aim was not to retest existing questions, but to address both the contextual aspect of income and its association with well-being as well as the relative aspect compared to local living standards all within a standardized set of robust measures (beyond the limited single-item measures used typically).

The primary objective was to provide a clearer pattern for the link between well-being and financial status (static and mobility) by looking at raw and relative incomes across countries while also factoring in the role of prior economic circumstances.
We took this approach to provide robust input on the link between financial circumstances and well-being, testing comprehensive measures from multiple approaches.
We also factored in concerning omissions about income thresholds in existing work.

Though our aim was understanding the role of relative income and economic history, we also provide consistent evidence that appears to validate and reconcile competing views on the income-well-being relationship, and a driving paradox in economic theory.
We use the data obtained by a previous study (Ruggeri et al., 2026), which provides estimates on selfreported sociodemographics, financial circumstances, and well-being across 92 countries.

text.text: Participants were recruited through a dynamic, multi-layered engagement approach.
They completed an online survey with questions about mental health, personal finances, and demographics.

All measures were translated and adapted to local contexts, including aligning all incomes to pre-tax, incorporating national indicators of GDP, and adding a relative cost of living value for each individual (described later; extensive details throughout Supplement 3).
An extensive data cleaning process removed responses that had either a significant number of flags or gave free-text responses that were simply implausible.
Exclusions were applied prior to or (naive to) analyses to avoid biasing the standard toward any particular result.
For the purposes of this study, we analyzed data in several ways.

To present general patterns, we present descriptive models that combine income (individual and national), multiple validated wellbeing measures, and various local standards to establish relative financial circumstances.
We used the 10-item multidimensional psychological well-being (MPWB) scale for the comprehensive well-being measure.
The scale can be used as individual measures, a sum score (ranging from 10 to 70), and as factor scores.
The factor scores can be estimated using either a global scale or as within-country scores that account for heterogeneity in responses between countries.
For robustness, all approaches were tested, though within-country factor scores are typically considered the most appropriate given income is largely a within-country construct.

We then ran a series of robust, inferential models to test the direct link between childhood SES (chSES), (relative) financial circumstances, and a composite, locally-standardized measure of psychological well-being.
Data involved approximately 52,000 participants for most analyses and 38,000 for those using chSES, which was an optional question with five categories (from "Poor" to "Wealthy").
Deviations for specific questions where values or participants were excluded or missing are detailed extensively in the supplementary materials.

Analyses proceeded through a progressive, structured model-building approach that iteratively relaxed the parametric constraints imposed on the data as warranted by formal model comparison and diagnostic evaluation.
For each research question, the variables were operationalized and transformed as appropriate for the specific modelling objective.
For example, a continuous measure of income was log-transformed to address skewness, and predictors were mean-centered in multilevel specifications to separate out between-and within-country effects.
Models were estimated sequentially, with increasing structural complexity.
Initial linear mixed models were extended, for example, to incorporate nonlinear smooths, random smooths, and factor-smooth country deviations where suitable.
These extensions allowed for the evaluation of the heterogeneity in the form and magnitude of the income-well-being associations under analysis.

Model selection relied on information criteria (e.g., AIC or BIC), variance explained (e.g., R²), and error metrics (e.g., RMSE), retaining models only for which formal comparisons indicated a significantly improved fit.
Where applicable, models accounted for the hierarchical country-level structure of the data, and observed nonlinearities were explicitly captured with multilevel generalized additive models.
This approach enabled the simultaneous estimation of both the global trends and country-specific heterogeneity in the functional form and magnitude of the effects.

A common criticism of this topic is that many studies on this topic rely on US data.
To provide insights on this, we also tested whether the relationship was unique for the US compared to other high-income countries.

Using multiple modeling approaches, there is evidence of a steeper-thanaverage association in the US compared to other high-income countries, though it is not an outlier (particularly when using the living wage ratios) nor does it have a distinct nonlinear shape relative to peer countries.
Furthermore, when accounting for unique heterogeneity within each country, this effect becomes very small and the US pattern falls well within the expected range of high-income variability.

Also, as will be noted later, the US does not have the strongest overall association, thus while it may be distinct from other high-income countries in the aggregate, it is not an outlier when compared to all countries individually.

Prior to any argument around income satiation -that is, the point at which money no longer measurably advances well-being identified by Kahneman and Deaton, among others -models must factor in not only an individual's current circumstance, but their previous economic standing and trajectory.
Though two adults may arrive at the same income, they may not have reached it in the same timeline or through the same means.
Likewise they are not guaranteed to relate to, spend, save, or otherwise leverage it in any homogenous way.
Put simply: the same $10 (or $100 or $1,000) can affect two lives in very different ways.
To account for this, we used a proxy of economic history by incorporating a measure of self-reported childhood socioeconomic status (chSES) into the models (see Figure 3, all panels).

Across multiple approaches, we find an unambiguous interaction for chSES: at all adult income deciles and incomes relative to costs, well-being is higher for individuals born into greater wealth.
Adults that have moved up significantly from childhood wealth consistently have lower well-being than those with wealthier chSES.

This is often true even if they out-earn those individuals as adults (e.g., an adult in the 9th decile from below-average chSES has lower well-being on average than someone from wealthy chSES in the 5th decile as an adult).
Concurrently, the income level for adults from low chSES to reach average well-being is significantly greater than those from high chSES.
In other words, to reach average national well-being, someone from a poor family may need to out-earn someone from a wealthy family by 5-10 times in adulthood.
Such outcomes are rare (see Supplement 2.7b).
We refer to this pattern, which holds strong relevance in subsequent findings, as "psychological inheritance."

We did not seek to validate or refute whether there is a satiation point where increased wealth is not associated with a substantive change in well-being, nor did we intend to align with any particular view supporting or opposing it.

Instead, we sought to model the role of income along with a multidimensional measure of well-being that factored in delineations for economic background and context, which is a problematic omission given our findings on chSES impacts.

Whether the climb from $50,000 to $60,000 is more significant on well-being than from $500,000 to $510,000 (equivalent increase) or even to $600,000 (proportional increase) may seem relevant to few, but as previous work inspired corporate initiatives to target satiation points (e.g., $75,000 base salaries), it is important that these are accurately reported.

text.text: At the inverse end of satiation, it is important also to ask if there are points at which no association between income and well-being exist.

This is particularly important to ask at a national level of countries with a significant absence of economic opportunity: if income is universally associated with well-being, then economic development is a requirement for any significant improvement.

Inversely, learning how individuals advance their own well-being in the absence of economic opportunity may offer substantial insights for effective policy, irrespective of national or individual wealth (our data were limited to test this aspect, but we have included a path for future research in Supplement 2.6b).
However, this may also be a heavily westernized framing, and critical dimensions of well-being, such as positive emotion, relationships, and self-esteem, are derived in entirely different ways.
Based on analyses of GDP, we find clearly diminishing associations between income and well-being, but stop short of absolute, national-wealth-driven decoupling (see Figure 6).

text.text: To test whether the income-well-being association weakens or collapses as a function of national wealth, we first estimated country-specific income-well-being slopes and plotted them against log GDP per capita.
Slopes were generally positive across the full range of GDP.
For countries under roughly US$10,000 GDP per capita, slopes were almost universally lower than 0.2.

Weaker slopes were also observed in countries with GDPs above $10,000 and even $50,000 per capita, leading us to conclude that while diminishing effects may be more common among lowerincome countries, such decoupling is not purely the result of limited national wealth.

Additionally, outliers such as Bahrain and UAE may be more reflective of distinct income distributions for disparate communities (e.g., professional class and migrant labor class) where the "richest poor person" may have greater well-being due to relative position and the "poorest rich person" may likewise be the inverse.
Both points would also explain why some patterns of stagnant well-being appear in economically advancing countries.
Rightly, most research on the role of economic mobility in well-being asks about the value of upward movement.
However, while often dismissed as non-critical (for understandable reasons), downward mobility may also reveal critical patterns for understanding and addressing national well-being.

text.text: First, higher chSES is universally associated with greater well-being within adult income groups (e.g., adults with above-average incomes born with above-average wealth have higher average well-being than adults with the same income born into average, low-income, and poor homes).
Second, any downward movement is associated with lower well-being compared to individuals who stayed in the higher income group as an adult.
Third, adults who move downward still have greater average well-being than individuals who started in lower chSES in the same group.

Thus, no amount of upward economic mobility matches the well-being of those who were born at the same level; any downward movement is associated with lower well-being than those who remained at the same level, but above those who started lower.
To complement those effects, we plot two additional mobility patterns in Figure 7.

text.text: The first approach shows how all upward mobility is associated with improvements in well-being compared to people who remained in the same income class as adults -effects are largest for those who increased most significantly.
The inverse is also true: the greatest declines are found in individuals with the furthest downward movement.

Collectively, the model produces a Simpson paradox: although higher income is clearly associated with greater well-being, it also creates larger opportunities for significant declines and fewer opportunities for upward movement (compared to low incomes) (see also Supplement 2.7c).
The second plot shows the average difference in well-being at each movement amount compared to individuals who remained in the chSES category on the LW dimension.
This shows a uniform trend of upward movement associated with better well-being and downward movement associated with worse.

However, the endowment also means the effect is still less than the difference in what was inherited initially.

In other words, even if the decline is larger, those who started off wealthy still end up with greater well-being than those with similar adult incomes. with worse well-being than those that remained.

text.text: To comprehensively test salient questions about that relationship using a broader set of measures that accounts for relative effects, we modelled the association between income and well-being using over 20 indicators from 53,589 people in 91countries.

Within those steps, we also included questions that would fill in gaps and account for debates about prevailing conclusions, then re-ran analyses to control for individual circumstances, such as local cost of living and economic history.

Through these analyses, we find an unambiguous, global (but not universal) positive association between income and well-being, where incomes around national averages and cost of living are highly elastic yet where the tails (absence or extreme) yield informative exceptions.
The nearly-uniform effects of economic mobility -in both directions -serve as further corroboration that income has an impact on well-being, which accelerates as it increases (or decreases).

With only minor exceptions, which were primarily nuances rather than deviations, findings aligned with primary hypotheses, which allow us to provide a unified narrative on the direct association with well-being.

Though consistent, we note the generally modest effect sizes in most analyses, indicating that while income is a strong predictor of well-being, it is not the only factor, and likely not among the most critical.
These would surely relate to matters such as physical health and safety, satisfaction of basic needs and security, as well as fundamental freedoms.

Yet, in using standardized scores of well-being, we can see clearly that income is far from irrelevant: modest changes income around local averages can shift an individual from having an overall negative to overall positive score, and the total ranges explained in some of our analyses cover as much as 20% of the total range in well-being.
This elasticity should reinforce the importance of personal finances in policymaking.
It was not our intention to identify specific income thresholds for happiness, but rather to focus on general trends.

However, we were generally compelled that across the World Bank income groups, a household income equivalent to approximately 4.5 times the living wage was the level at which wellbeing was reliably above average (see Supplement 3.2b).

This is potentially of extreme relevance to policymakers, employers, and individuals: below that value, individuals primarily exhibit belowaverage well-being at a time when global mental health is languishing (i.e., the average itself is generally low).
There are naturally exceptions to and deviations from the positive association between income and well-being, which are extremely informative.

First, it is clear that the relationship is strongest in higher-income locations: being low-income in a high-income area has a more negative relative association than having lower wealth in a poorer country.
Thus, upward movement in such countries shows a clear, positive effect on well-being, indicating a highly elastic relationship.
Of note, we do not find this to be uniquely or especially true in the US compared to other high-income countries.
Discouragingly, on average, no amount of upward movement can equate to always having wealth (Wang & Hanson, 2024).

Elasticities in well-being, however, can vary heavily in relation to costs of living.

At the top and bottom of income distributions for individuals and countries, there are clearly cases to be made for the existence of satiation (among the wealthiest individuals) and decoupling, which is visible in some locations but not limited to the lowest-income regions (Graham, 2009).

text.text: This is noteworthy in that it confirms that after reaching a certain level surpassing costs of living, the relationship is strongest.
Yet, above some levels of wealth, greater income may fail to offer increasing value toward well-being.

However, the level at which satiation appears to occur, we find, is substantially greater -and thus much harder to attain, particularly for those from lower initial wealth (Isaacs, 2007) or locations with fewer economic opportunities -than in previous findings.

text.text: Our goal in this study was not to redefine, resolve, or update satiation points; yet, confirming the existence of one along with some precision in real terms is immensely valuable for tangible policy recommendations that far exceed the standard but vacuous "good income" framing.
Across GDP groups, we find even average well-being is not typically reached until household incomes approach around 4.5 times the relative cost of living.
Not coincidentally, this point is near the middle of the most elastic points on the curve.
Though we urge discernment in how the exact number is treated, it was compelling in how it was so consistently observed across countries despite substantially heterogeneity in other analyses.

In unrelated work, using data from the Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), we had identified individuals at around the 67th percentile as being at the threshold for where optimal financial behaviors (e.g., maximized retirement savings) are observed (Federal Reserve, 2023).

text.text: A problem with pegging economic policy recommendations to percentiles is that, if incomes shift, percentiles change, and population mobility is zero-sum.
In further exploring our finding of 4.5 times living wage, we found that the two values were nearly identical when applied in real terms.
That is, where living wage was around 30,000, a household income of around 135,000 was typically in the 65th to 70th percentile.

Unlike percentiles, though, a multiplicative of a moving value provides a sustainable policy target for incomes that match the purpose of measuring GDP in the first place (i.e., estimating and inferring population well-being).
This overlap has motivated a new line of work to assess the validity of these values, as our data limit the extent to which we can do so.

Where weaker ties between income and well-being were observed, it seems evident that some individuals are able to generate at least some positive affect from their environment in the absence of sufficient financial resource and economic opportunity (Galbraith et al., 2024).

Given the limited number of individuals that move from lower chSES to significant wealth, satiation effects largely relate to those who have considerable wealth in childhood and are typically in a wealthier economic environment.
For lower chSES individuals, it is unsurprising that upward movement seems more likely to accelerate well-being.
This aligns with evidence that sudden financial windfalls produce greater positive affect in those worse-off (Dwyer & Dunn, 2022).

text.text: The loss of added (subjective) value from increased wealth is a privilege of those that have only known wealth, not of the positive deviant.
Such patterns make sense but also serve as a warning: while someone that has always and exclusively known wealth, added income offers little marginal value (or is at least highly inelastic).
Someone that has moved up significantly likely still has burdens not experienced by the former (e.g., student loans, financial care for older family members, lack of support networks).
Put bluntly: rich adults can still have poor parents.
Those effects do not disappear with a good paycheck and may even be impeded by unequal treatment despite being upwardly mobile (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?KTkcdJ. Sacks & Wolfers, 2010).

text.text: Policymakers need better frames to consider this.
Concurrently, the unambiguous effects for downward economic movement are a warning sign for regions of atrophying work opportunities.
While a significant psychological endowment may offer protective effects, not all downward movement starts from substantial wealth.

Instead, consider that the same effects are observed by those at all chSES: adults from middle and lower-middle class that do not secure similar economic opportunities as their parents are at risk of lower well-being across a significant number of years.

If young adults are unable to reach that income level and do not feel the prospects will change in the foreseeable future, our findings would indicate a significant decline across a large population is inevitable.
Nationally, our patterns provide strong evidence that country-level mobility in all directions can accelerate or impede population well-being.
Where there is greater wealth, it is unsurprising that wellbeing is higher.
But where economic opportunity is only recently expanding, it equally makes sense that upward national well-being may rise even faster in the short run.

Thus, rather than paradoxical, it is essentially systematic that when locations of great wealth experience cyclical or even seismic strains of economic opportunity at the individual level, there are simply more people capable of experiencing downward mobility.
If some continue to move up but movement does not significantly outpace any downward movement, national gains in well-being will not be experienced.
Our purpose in this manuscript was to present a robust argument about the limitations of income alone as an indicator of well-being when factoring in economic history.
We do not claim it is a perfectly robust dataset nor body of analyses.
Instead, we hope it presents a strong basis for further work, particularly studies that combine longitudinal and objective data as opposed to self-reported measures from a single collection.

text.text: Most relevant for this study, however, is that the analyses we present focus on large-group means and averages, thus they mainly offer a snapshot general trends at a moment in time.

As in all such approaches, they do not speak to individual experiences, outliers, exceptions, or "incomplete stories" (that is, their income, well-being, and other measures are a moment in time, not necessarily where they were yesterday or tomorrow or in ten years).

No one should therefore interpret these as absolute: of course there will be individuals that reach the middle class from poverty and find themselves far happier than those that have always been wealthy.

There will, tragically, always be people that have had objectively ideal circumstances that suffer from poor mental health, attempt suicide, or otherwise not experience the emotional privilege enjoyed by most in their economic class peers.
We therefore stress that our focus is general means; many deviations and exceptions absolutely exist and those neither verify nor invalidate what we conclude.
Additionally, it became clear that many existing disagreements on the topics in this article derive from differentiated approaches to data and analyses.
Decisions on whether to use log income, raw income, disposable income, and so on have direct and nonzero impacts on conclusions, to say the very least.

In fact, some of the strongest debates on this topic bluntly claim the alternate view is based on statistical shortcomings or artefacts (Dwyer & Dunn, 2022; Graham, 2010; D. W. Sacks et al., 2012; D. Sacks & Wolfers, 2010).

text.text: Though re-testing those debates was not our focus we aimed to avoid those issues by using a broad set of approaches to data and modelling but that also meant we avoided a straight-line approach of methods.
We also do not believe in a one-conclusion-fits-all interpretation of the link between income and well-being; there is clear heterogeneity within and between populations.
It may be that such ambivalence adds comprehensiveness at the expense of depth.
To that end, these data could be revisited with a predefined, narrow set of analytical guidelines, which may impact results.
Alternatively, the same approaches we use but applied to a different dataset may also impact conclusions.
We enthusiastically support all such (and other) attempts to test these effects using our arguments as a baseline.
We present an unambiguous link between income and well-being through comprehensive analyses incorporating multiple contextual measures of individual economic circumstances.

We conclude that the association is generally linear, though when adjusting income to account for costs of living, the pattern shifts to a log-linear relationship where elasticity is greatest as incomes pass living wage, but flatter at extremes.

Those findings appear to reconcile existing debates on the relationship, while noting the satiation point here, around thirty times the living wage, is significantly higher than others have reported and associated with extreme wealth.
Most critically and central to our primary interest, however, is that we find childhood wealth is a strong predictor of well-being in adults, particularly in countries with greater national wealth.
The greater the wealth someone is born into, the greater their well-being is likely to be as an adult, even if not achieving the same economic position.

Concurrently, the diminishing value of higher income is primarily a privilege of only the wealthiest; upward economic mobility will continue having value for the majority even if it will rarely be enough to flourish.
Policymakers concerned about national prosperity must heed these insights with urgency.
Similarly, employers now have a minimum target income level -around 4.5 times the local cost of living -if they generally wish for employees and their communities to flourish.

Ultimately, individuals have no choice over the families or environments they are born into, so investments must be made toward those factors that, at all levels, ages, and backgrounds, promote the well-being of the populations they serve.
